PHASE 4 · ADVANCED PRIMARY CARE CLINICAL MANAGEMENT

Week 88 — Lesson 112: Psoriasis & Psoriatic Arthritis

FNP-level goal: Recognize psoriasis as a chronic multisystem inflammatory disease, separate a limited stable plaque pattern from urgent pustular or erythrodermic illness, actively screen for psoriatic arthritis and cardiometabolic comorbidities, and coordinate skin, joint, and longitudinal primary-care management without overstepping systemic-treatment boundaries.

Learning Objectives

  • Recognize common psoriasis morphology and distinguish it from tinea, dermatitis, drug eruption, infection, and other inflammatory dermatoses.
  • Explain how immune-mediated inflammation creates plaque, nail, scalp, inverse, guttate, and pustular patterns and can extend beyond the skin.
  • Assess severity using body surface, special-site involvement, symptoms, quality of life, treatment burden, and functional limitation.
  • Screen deliberately for psoriatic arthritis, uveitis symptoms, cardiometabolic risk, mood disorders, inflammatory bowel disease history, and medication safety issues.
  • Recognize erythroderma, generalized pustular disease, severe systemic symptoms, acute joint compromise, and eye symptoms as escalation problems.

Part 1 — Psoriasis Is More Than a Plaque

Psoriasis is an immune-mediated inflammatory disease with visible skin manifestations and potential joint, cardiometabolic, and mental-health consequences. Plaque psoriasis commonly appears as sharply demarcated erythematous or hyperpigmented plaques with scale, often on extensor surfaces, scalp, and lumbosacral areas. Color and scale vary across skin tones, so texture, border, distribution, symptoms, and pigment change matter. A patient with less visible redness can still have highly active, painful, or stigmatizing disease.

The FNP should avoid two errors: treating psoriasis as a cosmetic issue, and treating every scaly plaque as psoriasis. Tinea can be annular with a more active border; dermatitis can be poorly defined and exposure-related; drug eruptions may be temporally related to a medication; bacterial or fungal infection can coexist. When the diagnosis is uncertain, lesions are atypical, or treatment repeatedly fails, reconsider the diagnosis and seek dermatologic help rather than simply increasing potency.

Part 2 — Mechanism and Clinical Patterns

Psoriatic inflammation accelerates keratinocyte turnover and drives vascular and immune changes, producing thick scale and plaques. The clinical pattern guides examination and referral. Scalp disease may be hidden but burdensome. Nail pitting, onycholysis, thickening, or crumbling can affect function and can also support the diagnosis. Inverse psoriasis affects folds and may have less scale because moisture changes surface appearance. Guttate disease may follow infections in some patients. Pustular and erythrodermic presentations can be systemically dangerous and should not be managed as ordinary outpatient plaque flares.

Triggers can include infection, physiologic stress, skin trauma, medication changes, alcohol, smoking, and withdrawal of systemic corticosteroids. Trigger review is not about blaming the patient; it helps identify modifiable factors and explains why sudden worsening may need a broader review of recent illness and medications.

Part 3 — Severity Is Not Just Body Surface Area

Body surface area helps quantify extent, but small areas can cause major disability. Hands, feet, scalp, face, genitals, nails, and intertriginous sites can interfere with work, mobility, intimacy, sleep, and self-image. Ask about itch, pain, fissures, bleeding, sleep, ability to wear shoes or gloves, occupational impact, sexual health, and depression or anxiety. A patient with limited palmoplantar plaques may be more functionally impaired than a patient with broader asymptomatic trunk disease.

Document the site, morphology, scale, fissures, nail findings, percent body surface estimate, symptoms, prior therapies, treatment access, and psychosocial effect. Photograph only with consent and secure storage. Baseline documentation supports meaningful follow-up because improvement can be incremental and chronic disease often waxes and wanes.

Part 4 — Screen for Psoriatic Arthritis at Every Opportunity

Psoriatic arthritis can occur before, with, or after skin disease and can cause irreversible joint damage if recognition is delayed. Ask specifically about swollen joints, prolonged morning stiffness, inflammatory back or buttock pain, heel pain, tendon insertion pain, dactylitis or a whole swollen digit, reduced hand function, nail changes, new fatigue, and functional decline. Do not assume all joint pain in a patient with psoriasis is osteoarthritis or weight-related mechanical pain.

Focused examination includes joints, digits, entheses when appropriate, range of motion, gait, spine symptoms, nail disease, and functional tasks. A positive structured screening tool can support further assessment but does not replace clinical judgment. New inflammatory joint symptoms, dactylitis, persistent swollen joints, or axial symptoms require rheumatology-oriented evaluation; early referral is a joint-protection intervention.

Part 5 — Comorbidities Are Part of the Diagnosis

Psoriasis is associated with higher burden of obesity, hypertension, dyslipidemia, diabetes, tobacco exposure, depression, anxiety, and cardiovascular risk. The FNP’s long-term role includes blood-pressure, lipid, glucose, weight, sleep, smoking, alcohol, and mental-health assessment according to current preventive-care standards and the patient’s priorities. Do not imply that cardiometabolic disease is caused by personal failure; frame risk reduction as part of treating inflammation and whole-person health.

Ask about eye pain, red eye, light sensitivity, or visual change, because inflammatory eye disease needs prompt evaluation. Ask about chronic diarrhea, blood in stool, abdominal pain, or known inflammatory bowel disease when symptoms suggest it. Coordinate rather than fragment care; dermatologic choices can interact with infection history, pregnancy plans, inflammatory bowel disease, hepatic disease, and other comorbidities.

Part 6 — Treatment Boundaries for Primary Care

For limited plaque disease, emollients, correct use of site-appropriate topical anti-inflammatory therapy, and selected steroid-sparing strategies are common components of care. Avoid treating face, folds, and genitals like thick chronic plaques on palms or soles; absorption and adverse-effect risk differ. Provide clear directions about site, amount, duration, expected benefit, and follow-up. Unstructured repeated refills can lead to undertreatment, steroid adverse effects, or delayed referral.

Phototherapy, conventional systemic agents, and biologics can be highly effective but require diagnosis confirmation, selection based on disease phenotype and comorbidities, baseline and ongoing safety evaluation, infection and vaccine planning, reproductive counseling when relevant, and specialist coordination. The FNP should not abruptly stop or change a specialist-directed systemic therapy without communication unless an emergency demands immediate action. Oral systemic corticosteroids should not be used casually as a psoriasis quick fix because abrupt changes and disease phenotype matter; coordinate with dermatology when systemic therapy is being considered.

Part 7 — Urgent Patterns

Generalized erythema with extensive skin involvement, fever, chills, dehydration, tachycardia, severe pain, widespread sterile pustules, new systemic illness, or a rapidly deteriorating patient may represent erythrodermic or generalized pustular psoriasis, severe infection, drug reaction, or another acute condition. These require urgent assessment. Similarly, a red painful eye with photophobia or visual change, acutely swollen joint with fever, or concern for septic arthritis is not managed as routine psoriasis follow-up.

Part 8 — Longitudinal Care and Referral

Dermatology referral is appropriate for uncertain diagnosis, severe or extensive disease, special-site disease with high impact, recurrent flares despite reasonable topical treatment, nail disease, need for phototherapy or systemic therapy, erythroderma or pustules, and significant quality-of-life burden. Rheumatology referral is appropriate for suspected psoriatic arthritis or inflammatory axial symptoms. Close the loop: document the reason, urgency, appointment status, specialist plan, safety labs or monitoring assigned to each clinician, and what the patient should do if symptoms worsen.

Part 9 — FNP Case: The Hands That Cannot Work

A grocery worker has plaques limited mainly to palms and fingertips, but fissures bleed with repetitive washing and lifting. Body surface area is low, yet pain, infection risk through fissures, and inability to work are high. The FNP treats severity as functional burden, confirms the diagnosis, builds a site-appropriate topical and barrier plan, assesses mood and work needs, and arranges dermatology follow-up rather than labeling the disease mild because the total area is small.

Part 10 — FNP Case: Skin Disease Plus Morning Stiffness

A patient with scalp and nail psoriasis reports two hours of morning hand stiffness, swollen fingers, and heel pain. The FNP recognizes an inflammatory pattern, documents joint and nail findings, screens for functional decline, orders only tests that answer a clinical question, and arranges prompt rheumatology evaluation. Joint symptoms are not an optional add-on to a dermatology visit.

Part 11 — FNP Case: The Patient Who Looks Ill

A patient with known psoriasis presents with diffuse painful erythema, widespread pustules, fever, and tachycardia after a medication change. The FNP does not simply prescribe a stronger topical agent. The differential includes severe psoriatic disease, infection, and drug reaction; the patient needs urgent evaluation and coordinated specialty care.

FNP High-Yield Framework: PLAQUE

  1. P — Pattern and phenotype: plaque, scalp, nail, inverse, guttate, pustular, or erythrodermic.
  2. L — Look beyond body surface: special sites, pain, sleep, work, sexual health, stigma, and mood.
  3. A — Ask about arthritis: inflammatory stiffness, swollen joints, dactylitis, enthesitis, back pain, and function.
  4. Q — Quantify comorbid risk: cardiometabolic health, smoking, mental health, eye symptoms, and bowel symptoms.
  5. U — Urgently escalate dangerous patterns: erythroderma, generalized pustules, systemic illness, eye symptoms, or acute joint concern.
  6. E — Engage specialists and track the plan: dermatology, rheumatology, and closed-loop follow-up.

Take-Home Summary

Psoriasis is chronic systemic inflammatory disease with skin, joint, metabolic, and psychological dimensions. FNP-level care recognizes morphology and mimics, measures functional impact as well as extent, screens for psoriatic arthritis and comorbidities, uses topical care safely, and escalates promptly for severe disease or inflammatory joint findings. The correct question is not only how much skin is involved, but how much health and function are being affected.

Educational note: This lesson supports clinical reasoning and does not replace a complete examination, current drug labeling, dermatology or rheumatology consultation, emergency care, or individualized treatment planning. Diffuse erythema, widespread pustules, fever, dehydration, severe pain, visual symptoms, or an acutely swollen joint requires urgent evaluation.
